claim: LP is the rodent homologue of primate pulvinar.
source: Lateral posterior nucleus (LP) of thalamus, the rodent homologue of primate pulvinar, projects extensively to sensory cortices.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature establishing this homology.

claim: LP projects extensively to sensory cortices.
source: Lateral posterior nucleus (LP) of thalamus, the rodent homologue of primate pulvinar, projects extensively to sensory cortices.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by anatomical tracing data shown in figures.

claim: LP improves auditory processing in A1 supragranular-layer neurons by sharpening their receptive fields and frequency tuning.
source: Here, bidirectional activity modulations of LP or its projection to the primary auditory cortex (A1) in awake mice reveal that LP improves auditory processing in A1 supragranular-layer neurons by sharpening their receptive fields and frequency tuning, as well as increasing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulations showing changes in frequency tuning bandwidth and SNR.

claim: LP increases the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of A1 supragranular-layer neurons.
source: Here, bidirectional activity modulations of LP or its projection to the primary auditory cortex (A1) in awake mice reveal that LP improves auditory processing in A1 supragranular-layer neurons by sharpening their receptive fields and frequency tuning, as well as increasing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing SNR changes with LP manipulation.

claim: LP modulation is achieved through a subtractive-suppression mechanism.
source: This is achieved through a subtractive-suppression mechanism, mediated largely by LP-to-A1 axons preferentially innervating specific inhibitory neurons in layer 1 and superficial layers.
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis showing positive/negative y-intercepts with slope near 1, and by circuit mapping data.

claim: LP-to-A1 axons preferentially innervate specific inhibitory neurons in layer 1 and superficial layers.
source: This is achieved through a subtractive-suppression mechanism, mediated largely by LP-to-A1 axons preferentially innervating specific inhibitory neurons in layer 1 and superficial layers.
evidence: Supported by slice recording data showing monosynaptic connections to L1 inhibitory neurons and PV neurons.

claim: LP is strongly activated by specific sensory signals relayed from the superior colliculus (SC).
source: LP is strongly activated by specific sensory signals relayed from the superior colliculus (SC), contributing to the maintenance and enhancement of A1 processing in the presence of auditory background noise and threatening visual looming stimuli respectively.
evidence: Supported by recording data showing LP responses to noise and visual stimuli, and by SC silencing experiments.

claim: LP contributes to the maintenance and enhancement of A1 processing in the presence of auditory background noise.
source: LP is strongly activated by specific sensory signals relayed from the superior colliculus (SC), contributing to the maintenance and enhancement of A1 processing in the presence of auditory background noise and threatening visual looming stimuli respectively.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing LP silencing effects on A1 responses under different noise conditions.

claim: LP contributes to the enhancement of A1 processing in the presence of threatening visual looming stimuli.
source: LP is strongly activated by specific sensory signals relayed from the superior colliculus (SC), contributing to the maintenance and enhancement of A1 processing in the presence of auditory background noise and threatening visual looming stimuli respectively.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing visual looming effects on A1 responses are blocked by LP silencing.

claim: A multisensory bottom-up SC-pulvinar-A1 pathway plays a role in contextual and cross-modality modulation of auditory cortical processing.
source: Thus, a multisensory bottom-up SC-pulvinar-A1 pathway plays a role in contextual and cross-modality modulation of auditory cortical processing.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing SC input to LP and LP modulation of A1 under different sensory contexts.

claim: First-order thalamic nuclei serve as the major driver of sensory responses in the cortex for each respective sensory modality.
source: They serve as the major driver of sensory responses in the cortex for each respective sensory modality (Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Halassa and Sherman, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The functional roles of higher-order thalamic nuclei in sensory processing are much less well understood compared to first-order thalamic nuclei.
source: Compared to first-order thalamic nuclei, the functional roles of higher-order thalamic nuclei in sensory processing are much less well understood, although many of them are known to have broad connections with both primary and secondary cortices.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: LP/pulvinar is considered the largest thalamic complex.
source: The latter is considered the largest thalamic complex (Harting et al., 1973).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies on LP/pulvinar have mostly been focused on its involvement in visual-related functions.
source: Previous studies on LP/pulvinar have mostly been focused on its involvement in visual-related functions, such as visual attention, visually guided behaviors and eye movements (Dominguez-Vargas et al., 2017; Saalmann et al., 2012; Soares et al., 2017; Stitt et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2016), largely due to its extensive reciprocal connections with visual cortical areas (Beltramo and Scanziani, 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Juavinett et al., 2020; Kaas and Lyon, 2007; Nakamura et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2014; Roth et al., 2016; Shipp, 2001; Stitt et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: LP/pulvinar has connections with primary and secondary auditory cortices.
source: Besides visual cortices, LP/pulvinar also has connections with other sensory cortices including primary and secondary auditory cortices (Cappe et al., 2009; Hackett et al., 1998; Nakamura et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2014; Shipp, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: LP contains auditory responsive neurons which exhibit short-latency responses.
source: and contains auditory responsive neurons which exhibit short-latency responses (Chalupa and Fish, 1978; Gattass et al., 1978; Magariños-Ascone et al., 1988; Woody et al., 1991; Yirmiya and Hocherman, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: The influence of LP on auditory cortical responses has rarely been examined.
source: However, the influence of LP on auditory cortical responses has rarely been examined.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field.

claim: Axonal projections from LP to primary sensory cortices mainly terminate in layer 1.
source: It is known that the axonal projections from LP to primary sensory cortices mainly terminate in layer 1 (L1), whereas those to secondary sensory cortices mainly terminate in L4 (Fang et al., 2020; Roth et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Axonal projections from LP to secondary sensory cortices mainly terminate in L4.
source: It is known that the axonal projections from LP to primary sensory cortices mainly terminate in layer 1 (L1), whereas those to secondary sensory cortices mainly terminate in L4 (Fang et al., 2020; Roth et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: L1 contains predominantly inhibitory neurons.
source: As L1 contains predominantly inhibitory neurons (Jiang et al., 2013; Mesik et al., 2019; Schuman et al., 2019), it is likely that the LP input to the primary sensory cortex plays some modulatory roles.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on L1 composition.

claim: LP input to the primary sensory cortex likely plays some modulatory roles.
source: As L1 contains predominantly inhibitory neurons (Jiang et al., 2013; Mesik et al., 2019; Schuman et al., 2019), it is likely that the LP input to the primary sensory cortex plays some modulatory roles.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical knowledge about L1 and LP projection patterns.

claim: Silencing LP increased the spontaneous firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Analyzing all the recorded L2/3 neurons, we found significant increases in the spontaneous firing rate (FR), evoked FR and bandwidth of frequency tuning (as measured at an intensity level of 60 dB SPL and at 20 dB above the intensity threshold) when silencing LP (Figure 1D–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Silencing LP increased the evoked firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Analyzing all the recorded L2/3 neurons, we found significant increases in the spontaneous firing rate (FR), evoked FR and bandwidth of frequency tuning (as measured at an intensity level of 60 dB SPL and at 20 dB above the intensity threshold) when silencing LP (Figure 1D–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Silencing LP increased the bandwidth of frequency tuning of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Analyzing all the recorded L2/3 neurons, we found significant increases in the spontaneous firing rate (FR), evoked FR and bandwidth of frequency tuning (as measured at an intensity level of 60 dB SPL and at 20 dB above the intensity threshold) when silencing LP (Figure 1D–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Silencing LP reduced the signal-to-noise ratio of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: More importantly, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), as measured by the ratio of evoked to spontaneous FR, was reduced (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Silencing LP did not change the characteristic frequency of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Nevertheless, the overall shape of frequency tuning (Figure 1C) and the CF of TRF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) were largely preserved.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Activation of LP reduced the spontaneous firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Opposite to the effects of silencing LP, activation of LP reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, and narrowed the frequency tuning bandwidth, while enhancing the SNR (Figure 1K–N; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Activation of LP reduced the evoked firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Opposite to the effects of silencing LP, activation of LP reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, and narrowed the frequency tuning bandwidth, while enhancing the SNR (Figure 1K–N; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Activation of LP narrowed the frequency tuning bandwidth of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Opposite to the effects of silencing LP, activation of LP reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, and narrowed the frequency tuning bandwidth, while enhancing the SNR (Figure 1K–N; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Activation of LP enhanced the signal-to-noise ratio of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Opposite to the effects of silencing LP, activation of LP reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, and narrowed the frequency tuning bandwidth, while enhancing the SNR (Figure 1K–N; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1N.

claim: Activation of LP did not change the characteristic frequency of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: without changing the CF (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: LP did not have modulatory effects on A1 L4 neurons.
source: In L4, we did not observe any changes of either spontaneous or evoked FR induced by optogenetic manipulations of LP (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The LP's modulatory effect may be specific to superficial layers.
source: Therefore, the LP's modulatory effect may be specific to superficial layers.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that L4 neurons were not affected by LP manipulation.

claim: LP modulation exhibits a subtractive-suppression-like effect with a slope close to 1 in linear regression analysis.
source: The slope of the best fit line was close to 1 for both LP silencing and activation (Figure 1R), suggesting that there was no change in the response gain (i.e. no evidence for a multiplicative effect).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 1R.

claim: LP silencing produced a positive y-intercept in linear regression analysis of tone responses.
source: The y-intercept was all positive for LP silencing but negative for LP activation (Figure 1S).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 1S.

claim: LP activation produced a negative y-intercept in linear regression analysis of tone responses.
source: The y-intercept was all positive for LP silencing but negative for LP activation (Figure 1S).
evidence: Supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 1S.

claim: LP modulation is similar to a thresholding effect produced by increasing the level of background noise.
source: These results strongly suggest a subtractive-suppression-like modulation of A1 responses by LP activity, similar to a thresholding effect produced by increasing the level of background noise (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on the pattern of results and comparison to previous literature.

claim: Numerous LP neurons project to A1.
source: Numerous retrogradely labeled neurons were found in LP (Figure 2A, right), with a bias towards its caudal part (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LP neurons projecting to A1 are biased towards the caudal part of LP.
source: Numerous retrogradely labeled neurons were found in LP (Figure 2A, right), with a bias towards its caudal part (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LP axons densely innervate L1 and deep layers of A1.
source: Furthermore, injection of AAV-GFP into LP revealed densely labeled axon terminals in L1 as well as deep layers of A1 (Figure 2B), confirming the direct projection from LP to A1 (De La Mothe et al., 2006; Nakamura et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Silencing LP-A1 axon terminals increased the spontaneous firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We observed effects on A1 L2/3 neurons similar to silencing LP neurons per se: the spontaneous and evoked FR was increased, the frequency tuning bandwidth was broadened, and the SNR was reduced (Figure 2D–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Silencing LP-A1 axon terminals increased the evoked firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We observed effects on A1 L2/3 neurons similar to silencing LP neurons per se: the spontaneous and evoked FR was increased, the frequency tuning bandwidth was broadened, and the SNR was reduced (Figure 2D–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Silencing LP-A1 axon terminals broadened the frequency tuning bandwidth of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We observed effects on A1 L2/3 neurons similar to silencing LP neurons per se: the spontaneous and evoked FR was increased, the frequency tuning bandwidth was broadened, and the SNR was reduced (Figure 2D–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Silencing LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the signal-to-noise ratio of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: We observed effects on A1 L2/3 neurons similar to silencing LP neurons per se: the spontaneous and evoked FR was increased, the frequency tuning bandwidth was broadened, and the SNR was reduced (Figure 2D–G; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Activating LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the spontaneous firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In line with the effects caused by LP activation, the activation of LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, sharpened frequency tuning, and enhanced the SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2I–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Activating LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the evoked firing rate of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In line with the effects caused by LP activation, the activation of LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, sharpened frequency tuning, and enhanced the SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2I–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Activating LP-A1 axon terminals sharpened frequency tuning of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In line with the effects caused by LP activation, the activation of LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, sharpened frequency tuning, and enhanced the SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2I–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Activating LP-A1 axon terminals enhanced the signal-to-noise ratio of A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In line with the effects caused by LP activation, the activation of LP-A1 axon terminals reduced the spontaneous and evoked FR, sharpened frequency tuning, and enhanced the SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2I–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The LP to A1 projection largely mediates the LP modulatory effect on A1 responses.
source: These data suggest that the LP to A1 projection largely mediates the LP modulatory effect on A1 responses.
evidence: Inference based on the similarity of effects between LP soma and LP terminal manipulations.

claim: The LP projection to the cortex per se is excitatory.
source: As the LP projection to the cortex per se is excitatory (Evangelio et al., 2018; Roth et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018), an immediate question is how LP activity exerts a net inhibitory effect on A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: None of the recorded pyramidal neurons across L2-4 received direct input from LP.
source: Overall, none of the PYR neurons we recorded across L2-4 received direct input from LP, whereas more than 50% of L1 inhibitory neurons received direct LP input (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: Supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3C and E.

claim: More than 50% of L1 inhibitory neurons received direct LP input.
source: Overall, none of the PYR neurons we recorded across L2-4 received direct input from LP, whereas more than 50% of L1 inhibitory neurons received direct LP input (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: Supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A similar fraction of PV neurons in L2/3 received direct input from LP as L1 inhibitory neurons.
source: A similar fraction of PV neurons in L2/3 received direct input from LP, whereas none of the recorded SOM neurons did so (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: None of the recorded SOM neurons received direct input from LP.
source: A similar fraction of PV neurons in L2/3 received direct input from LP, whereas none of the recorded SOM neurons did so (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A much smaller fraction of PV neurons in L4 received LP input compared to L2/3 PV neurons.
source: A much smaller fraction of PV neurons in L4 also received LP input (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: LP-A1 axons preferentially innervate L1 inhibitory neurons and superficial-layer PV inhibitory neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate that LP-A1 axons preferentially innervate L1 inhibitory neurons and superficial-layer PV inhibitory neurons, which may then provide disynaptic inhibition to L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from slice recording data showing connection patterns.

claim: L1 inhibitory neurons and superficial-layer PV inhibitory neurons may provide disynaptic inhibition to L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Together, these results indicate that LP-A1 axons preferentially innervate L1 inhibitory neurons and superficial-layer PV inhibitory neurons, which may then provide disynaptic inhibition to L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: Inference based on connectivity patterns and known circuit properties.

claim: LP neurons responded robustly to white-noise sound.
source: We noticed that LP neurons responded robustly to white-noise sound, with the response amplitude increasing with increasing noise levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by recording data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: LP neuron response amplitude to white noise increases with increasing noise levels.
source: We noticed that LP neurons responded robustly to white-noise sound, with the response amplitude increasing with increasing noise levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by recording data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The superior colliculus (SC) innervates LP.
source: Previous anatomical and electrophysiological studies have shown that the superior colliculus (SC) in the midbrain innervates LP (Beltramo and Scanziani, 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020; Gale and Murphy, 2014; Stepniewska et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2015; Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The onset latency of noise responses was shortest in SC compared to LP and A1 L4.
source: Comparing the onset latency of noise responses in SC, LP, and A1 L4, we found that it was the shortest in SC, while similar between LP and A1 L4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The onset latency of noise responses was similar between LP and A1 L4.
source: Comparing the onset latency of noise responses in SC, LP, and A1 L4, we found that it was the shortest in SC, while similar between LP and A1 L4 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by recording data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The responses in LP are unlikely due to feedback inputs from auditory cortices.
source: This suggests that the responses in LP (at least the early part) are unlikely due to feedback inputs from auditory cortices.
evidence: Inference based on latency comparison data.

claim: Silencing SC greatly reduced the amplitude of noise responses in LP.
source: Furthermore, silencing SC greatly reduced the amplitude of noise responses in LP (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The noise responses in LP are primarily driven by bottom-up input likely from SC.
source: Our results thus indicate that the noise responses in LP are primarily driven by bottom-up input likely from SC.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from latency and SC silencing experiments.

claim: Increasing the noise level reduced the amplitude of the response evoked by the best-frequency tone in A1 L2/3 neurons.
source: As shown by an example A1 L2/3 neuron (Figure 4D and E, gray), increasing the noise level reduced the amplitude of the response evoked by the best-frequency tone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Silencing LP universally enhanced tone-evoked responses in A1 across different noise levels.
source: Summarizing all the recorded L2/3 neurons, we found that silencing LP universally enhanced tone-evoked responses in A1 across different noise levels (Figure 4F, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The enhancement of tone-evoked responses by LP silencing was larger at higher noise levels.
source: Notably, the enhancement was larger at higher noise levels (Figure 4F, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Silencing LP elevated the spontaneous firing rate in a noise-level dependent manner.
source: Silencing LP also elevated the spontaneous FR in a noise-level dependent manner so that the elevation was larger at higher noise levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: High-level noise has a detrimental effect on SNR in A1 neurons.
source: The SNR slightly decreased with increasing noise levels in the control condition (Figure 4H, upper panel, black), indicating that high-level noise has a detrimental effect on SNR, thus deteriorating auditory processing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Silencing LP not only reduced SNR, but also accelerated the detrimental effect of background noise.
source: Silencing LP not only reduced SNR, but also accelerated the detrimental effect of background noise (Figure 4H, upper panel, red).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The frequency tuning bandwidth was reduced with increasing noise levels.
source: Finally, the frequency tuning bandwidth was reduced with increasing noise levels (Figure 4I, upper panel), consistent with previous studies (Ehret and Schreiner, 2000; Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and citations to previous studies.

claim: Silencing LP broadened the tuning bandwidth.
source: Silencing LP not only broadened the tuning bandwidth, but also slowed down the modulation of tuning bandwidth by increasing the noise level (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Silencing LP slowed down the modulation of tuning bandwidth by increasing the noise level.
source: Silencing LP not only broadened the tuning bandwidth, but also slowed down the modulation of tuning bandwidth by increasing the noise level (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: LP plays a role in contextual modulation of A1 frequency processing by noise background.
source: Together, these results suggest that LP plays a role in contextual modulation of A1 frequency processing by noise background.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing LP effects under different noise conditions.

claim: SC does not project to auditory cortices.
source: Since SC innervates LP (Beltramo and Scanziani, 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Gale and Murphy, 2014; Stepniewska et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2015; Zingg et al., 2017) but does not project to auditory cortices (Basso and May, 2017; Cang et al., 2018; Ito and Feldheim, 2018), we wondered whether SC could provide direct input to drive the LP-mediated modulation of A1 responses.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Abundant GFP-labeled axons from SC were found in LP.
source: We found abundant GFP-labeled axons in LP (Figure 5A), with a strong bias towards its caudal part (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SC axons in LP have a strong bias towards the caudal part of LP.
source: We found abundant GFP-labeled axons in LP (Figure 5A), with a strong bias towards its caudal part (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SC axons directly innervate LP neurons.
source: Expressing ChR2 in intermediate and deep layers of SC and then performing whole-cell slice recording from caudal LP neurons in the presence of TTX and 4AP further confirmed direct innervations of LP neurons by SC axons (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by slice recording data showing monosynaptic connections in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SC neurons decreased spontaneous firing rates in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of these SC neurons induced effects on A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons similar to activation of LP: spontaneous and evoked firing rates were decreased, and SNR was increased (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SC neurons decreased evoked firing rates in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of these SC neurons induced effects on A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons similar to activation of LP: spontaneous and evoked firing rates were decreased, and SNR was increased (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SC neurons increased SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Optogenetic activation of these SC neurons induced effects on A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons similar to activation of LP: spontaneous and evoked firing rates were decreased, and SNR was increased (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SC-recipient LP neurons reduced spontaneous firing rates in A1 L2/3 neurons.
source: In A1, optogenetic activation of SC-recipient LP neurons produced similar effects to the activation of the general LP population: spontaneous and evoked firing rates were reduced, and SNR was increased (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SC-recipient LP neurons reduced evoked firing rates in A1 L2/3 neurons.
source: In A1, optogenetic activation of SC-recipient LP neurons produced similar effects to the activation of the general LP population: spontaneous and evoked firing rates were reduced, and SNR was increased (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SC-recipient LP neurons increased SNR in A1 L2/3 neurons.
source: In A1, optogenetic activation of SC-recipient LP neurons produced similar effects to the activation of the general LP population: spontaneous and evoked firing rates were reduced, and SNR was increased (Figure 5I–K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Silencing SC resulted in increases of spontaneous firing rates in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: This resulted in increases of spontaneous and evoked firing rates, broadening of frequency tuning and a reduction of SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5M–P), similar to silencing LP per se.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5M.

claim: Silencing SC resulted in increases of evoked firing rates in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: This resulted in increases of spontaneous and evoked firing rates, broadening of frequency tuning and a reduction of SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5M–P), similar to silencing LP per se.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Silencing SC resulted in broadening of frequency tuning in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: This resulted in increases of spontaneous and evoked firing rates, broadening of frequency tuning and a reduction of SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5M–P), similar to silencing LP per se.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Silencing SC resulted in a reduction of SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: This resulted in increases of spontaneous and evoked firing rates, broadening of frequency tuning and a reduction of SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5M–P), similar to silencing LP per se.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5P.

claim: SC can provide input to drive LP-mediated modulation of A1 responses.
source: Together, these results provide supporting evidence that SC can provide input to drive LP-mediated modulation of A1 responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing SC effects on A1 via LP.

claim: Both SC and LP process visual information.
source: Both SC and LP process visual information and have been implicated in visual looming stimuli induced defensive behaviors such as freezing (Wei et al., 2015; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013; Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SC and LP have been implicated in visual looming stimuli induced defensive behaviors such as freezing.
source: Both SC and LP process visual information and have been implicated in visual looming stimuli induced defensive behaviors such as freezing (Wei et al., 2015; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013; Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Directly stimulating superficial-layer SC neurons can elicit freezing responses in mice.
source: Directly stimulating superficial-layer SC neurons, which receive visual input (Zhao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017), can elicit freezing responses in mice (Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: LP neurons responded more strongly to visual looming stimuli compared to grating and noise-pattern stimuli.
source: Notably, LP neurons responded more strongly to visual looming stimuli compared to more commonly used grating and noise-pattern stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Visual looming stimuli reduced spontaneous firing rates in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In the presence of visual looming stimuli, spontaneous and evoked firing rates were reduced (Figure 6B and C), while the SNR was increased (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Visual looming stimuli reduced evoked firing rates in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In the presence of visual looming stimuli, spontaneous and evoked firing rates were reduced (Figure 6B and C), while the SNR was increased (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Visual looming stimuli increased SNR in A1 L2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In the presence of visual looming stimuli, spontaneous and evoked firing rates were reduced (Figure 6B and C), while the SNR was increased (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Visual looming stimuli can modulate A1 responses.
source: These results indicate that visual looming stimuli can indeed modulate A1 responses.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data showing changes in A1 responses with visual looming.

claim: Silencing LP blocked the effects on A1 responses by visual looming stimuli.
source: After silencing LP with muscimol (Figure 6E), the effects on A1 responses by visual looming stimuli disappeared (Figure 6F–H), suggesting that LP primarily mediates the visual looming stimuli induced modulation of auditory responses in A1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: LP primarily mediates the visual looming stimuli induced modulation of auditory responses in A1.
source: After silencing LP with muscimol (Figure 6E), the effects on A1 responses by visual looming stimuli disappeared (Figure 6F–H), suggesting that LP primarily mediates the visual looming stimuli induced modulation of auditory responses in A1.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing LP silencing blocks visual looming effects.

claim: The overall outcome of increasing LP activity is to improve auditory processing by sharpening frequency tuning and enhancing SNR of auditory evoked responses.
source: In the present study, our results demonstrate that LP activity can modulate auditory processing in superficial layers of A1. The overall outcome of increasing LP activity is to improve auditory processing by sharpening frequency tuning and enhancing SNR of auditory evoked responses.
evidence: Summary statement supported by multiple experimental results.

claim: LP modulation is achieved by subtractive suppression of auditory evoked responses together with suppression of spontaneous firing activity.
source: This is achieved by subtractive suppression of auditory evoked responses together with suppression of spontaneous firing activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from linear regression analysis and experimental data.

claim: The suppression of A1 L2/3 responses by LP is consistent with a similar suppressive effect in L2/3 of the primary visual cortex (V1).
source: The suppression of A1 L2/3 responses is consistent with our recent study showing a similar suppressive effect in L2/3 of the primary visual cortex (V1), which results in an enhancement of visual feature selectivity (Fang et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison to previous study by the same authors.

claim: L1 inhibitory neurons may be broadly tuned for frequency.
source: The subtractive effect on L2/3 responses suggests that L1 inhibitory neurons (and PV neurons in superficial layers as well) may be broadly tuned for frequency.
evidence: Inference based on the subtractive effect observed in the data.

claim: L1 inhibitory neurons in the visual cortex are broadly tuned for visual features such as orientation and direction.
source: The frequency tuning property of L1 inhibitory neurons in the auditory cortex has not been studied yet, but a previous study in the visual cortex does suggest that L1 inhibitory neurons are broadly tuned for visual features such as orientation and direction (Mesik et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study in visual cortex.

claim: PV neurons in superficial layers of A1 have been shown to be broadly tuned for tone frequency.
source: and PV neurons in superficial layers of A1 have been shown to be broadly tuned for tone frequency (Cohen and Mizrahi, 2015; Li et al., 2015; Liang et al., 2019; Maor et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both L1 inhibitory neurons and L2/3 PV neurons can directly inhibit L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: As for the local circuit involved, we suggest that both L1 inhibitory neurons and L2/3 PV neurons, which receive direct LP input, can directly inhibit L2/3 pyramidal cells (Jiang et al., 2013), generating an overall suppressive effect.
evidence: Inference based on connectivity data and citation to previous study.

claim: 70% of L1 inhibitory neurons are NDNF+.
source: For L1 inhibitory neurons, their molecular identities have been reported to be diverse: 70% are NDNF+, 20% are nAchR+, and 10% are VIP+ (Schuman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: 20% of L1 inhibitory neurons are nAchR+.
source: For L1 inhibitory neurons, their molecular identities have been reported to be diverse: 70% are NDNF+, 20% are nAchR+, and 10% are VIP+ (Schuman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: 10% of L1 inhibitory neurons are VIP+.
source: For L1 inhibitory neurons, their molecular identities have been reported to be diverse: 70% are NDNF+, 20% are nAchR+, and 10% are VIP+ (Schuman et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The LP-mediated modulatory effect on A1 processing may be particularly pronounced and beneficial when there is a high noise background.
source: The LP-mediated modulatory effect on A1 processing may be particularly pronounced and beneficial when there is a high noise background.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing noise-level dependent effects.

claim: Increasing background noise is equivalent to lowering the intensity of test stimuli.
source: A previous study has demonstrated that increasing background noise is equivalent to lowering the intensity of test (e.g. tone) stimuli, that is, shifting up the TRF by a certain Δthreshold value (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The noise effect on A1 frequency tuning may be achieved, at least partially, through LP.
source: Our results suggest that the noise effect on A1 frequency tuning may be achieved, at least partially, through LP.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results showing LP effects under noise conditions.

claim: LP/pulvinar has extensive reciprocal connectivity with cortical areas including visual and auditory cortices.
source: It is known that LP/pulvinar has extensive reciprocal connectivity with cortical areas including visual and auditory cortices (Hackett et al., 1998; De La Mothe et al., 2006; Nakamura et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2014; Tohmi et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2018; Bennett et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LP/pulvinar serves in a cortico-thalamo-cortical ('transthalamic') indirect route for information transfer from one cortical area to another.
source: Previously, it has been suggested that LP/pulvinar serves in a cortico-thalamo-cortical ('transthalamic') indirect route for information transfer from one cortical area to another (Guillery and Sherman, 2002; Sherman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: LP receives strong inputs from SC.
source: Besides cortical inputs, LP also receive strong inputs from SC (Beltramo and Scanziani, 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020; Gale and Murphy, 2014; Stepniewska et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2015; Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LP (mainly the caudal part) receives direct input from the auditory related part of SC.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that LP (mainly the caudal part) receives direct input from the auditory related part of SC and projects to A1, and that silencing SC produces changes in A1 functional response properties similar to silencing LP.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing and functional experiments.

claim: SC can relay bottom-up input to LP to drive its modulation of A1 processing.
source: These results together suggest that SC can relay bottom-up input to LP to drive its modulation of A1 processing.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing SC-LP-A1 pathway.

claim: SC is a multisensory structure.
source: In addition, SC is a multisensory structure (Drager and Hubel, 1975; King and Palmer, 1985; Meredith and Stein, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The superficial layer of SC projects strongly to the caudal LP.
source: The visual only part of SC, that is the superficial layer of SC, also projects strongly to the caudal LP (Beltramo and Scanziani, 2019; Bennett et al., 2019; Fang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The multisensory nature of SC and its strong projections to LP potentially endow LP with an ability to modulate A1 activity given any salient sensory stimuli.
source: We postulate that the multisensory nature of SC and its strong projections to LP potentially endow LP with an ability to modulate A1 activity given any salient sensory stimuli.
evidence: Speculation based on the experimental findings and known properties of SC.

claim: A previously unrecognized pathway, the SC-LP-A1 pathway, can provide contextual and cross-modality modulation of A1 responses and auditory processing to enhance the salience of acoustic information.
source: In summary, our results suggest that a previously unrecognized pathway, the SC-LP-A1 pathway, can provide contextual and cross-modality modulation of A1 responses and auditory processing to enhance the salience of acoustic information.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from all experimental results.
